abstract: Abstract The development of a generic drug product involves demonstrating that there is no significant difference in the rate and extent to which the active ingredient becomes available at the site of action, relative to the reference listed drug product. This remains challenging for many locally acting topical dermatological products because measuring the concentration of the active ingredient at the site of action in the skin may not be straightforward, and, in most instances, there are no established relationships between skin and plasma pharmacokinetic profiles. In recent years, the Office of Generic Drugs of the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) established scientific research programs with the goal of enhancing patient access to high quality, affordable topical dermatological generics. A key strategy of these research programs was to leverage modeling and simulation methodologies that accelerate the development of these generics by facilitating alternative bioequivalence approaches for dermatological drug products. This report summarizes relevant insights and discussions from a 2021 FDA public workshop titled “Regulatory Utility of Mechanistic Modeling to Support Alternative Bioequivalence Approaches,” which illustrated how mechanistic modeling and simulation approaches can be utilized (and have been used) to inform generic drug product development and regulatory decisions during the assessment of generic drug applications submitted to the FDA.
body:
INTRODUCTION
Drug products may be applied on the skin with the intention to act locally following (topical) delivery of the active ingredient to the skin, itself, or with the intention to act systemically following (transdermal) delivery of the active ingredient through the skin.
1
,
2
Per the Generic Drug User Fee Amendments (GDUFA) II commitment letter, topical drug products intended for local action (mostly semisolid dosage forms) are considered complex drug products primarily because they involve a complex route of delivery and complex dosage forms.
3
Studies recommended by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for establishing the bioequivalence (BE) of these products include, but are not limited to, physicochemical and structural (Q3) characterizations of the drug product, in vitro release testing (IVRT) and in vitro permeation testing (IVPT) studies, in vivo studies with a pharmacodynamic end point (vasoconstrictor studies), in vivo studies with pharmacokinetic (PK) end points, and comparative clinical end point BE studies.
4
,
5
Unlike many systemically acting generic drug products, for which BE has traditionally been demonstrated based upon in vivo PK studies that efficiently monitor the rate and extent to which active ingredients become available in the blood of healthy subjects, BE for locally acting (topical dermatological) generic drug products has traditionally relied upon comparative clinical end point BE studies in patients because of challenges with monitoring the rate and extent to which the active ingredient becomes available in the skin. However, comparative clinical end point BE studies are typically lengthy (with end points measured after several weeks to months), costly (involving large numbers of patients), risky (because of challenges with demonstrating superiority over placebo vehicles), and may not be the most sensitive and discriminating approach by which to demonstrate BE.
4
,
5
To support regulatory decision making for dermatological drug products applied to the skin, science and research supported by GDUFA I and II has focused on regulatory outcomes.
4
Recently, the development and incorporation into product‐specific guidances (PSGs) of efficient BE approaches have led to the approval of high quality generic topical dermatological drug products, as reported by Raney et al., 2020.
5
These novel BE approaches include in vitro BE studies and characterization tests that are used to reliably compare the generic to the reference listed drug product.
2
Quantitative methodologies, such as physiologically‐based PK (PBPK) modeling, have been one of the main areas of focus for FDA's GDUFA research program since its inception, and the first grant in the dermal area was awarded in 2014 with several to follow.
4
,
6
,
7
The overall goal of these grants, listed in Table
1
, has been to develop in silico tools that would allow for a mechanistic description of the skin permeation of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) following administration of dermatological drug products in virtual subjects of healthy and diseased populations.
8
,
9
,
10
,
11
,
12
These PBPK models incorporate drug product attributes allowing for product‐specific predictions of the in vivo performance of that drug product. Importantly, by accounting for product quality attributes and the formulation‐skin physiology interactions, the application of these models is not only useful in making informed decisions during the product development program, but also supporting alternative BE approaches on a case‐by‐case basis.
13

The current state of using mechanistic modeling and simulation to support generic product development and alternative BE approaches for dermatological drug products was extensively discussed at a recent FDA public workshop titled “Regulatory Utility of Mechanistic Modeling to Support Alternative Bioequivalence Approaches,”
14
cohosted online with the Center for Complex Generics (CRCG), on September 30 through October 1, 2021. This report summarizes the podium presentations and panel discussion from the workshop's Symposium I: “Mechanistic Modeling of Locally‐Acting Generic Drug Products,” Session 2: “Mechanistic modeling of dermal generic drug products.”
OVERALL SUMMARY
Moderated by Drs. Sam Raney (FDA) and Sumit Arora (Janssen), the workshop session included five presentations designed to communicate to relevant stakeholders from the generic drug industry, academia, and other regulatory agencies that modeling and simulation methodologies can be leveraged to inform decisions within the scope of a drug product development program and to support regulatory decision making. One important message from speakers representing modeling software developers (Dr. Jessica Spires [Simulations Plus] and Dr. Sebastian Polak [Certara, Simcyp]) was that, to date, the development and performance assessment of in silico models has relied largely on information and data generated as part of the in vitro characterization of the reference listed drug product, as well as on in vitro and in vivo data generated by the applicant to support their development program and their regulatory submission (i.e., IVPT study data and clinical PK data from an in vivo BE study with PK end points, as well as data obtained from literature sources). Therefore, data needed for model development and validation, are largely already available from studies routinely performed within the scope of a generic development program, and the burden of any additional experimental studies that may be needed for model development and validation is expected to be low. Their talks also highlighted that PBPK models for dermatological drug products rely on the knowledge and experience gained through modeling and simulation of other drugs and drug products. The objective of the talks by the FDA speakers (Drs. Khondoker Alam, Priyanka Ghosh, and Eleftheria Tsakalozou) was to illustrate how these tools are currently used to support internal decision making by the FDA as well as to support regulatory decisions relating to generic drug product approval.
During the panel discussion, speakers and Drs. Lanyan Fang (FDA), Srinivasa Sammeta (Teva), and Ping Zhao (Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation) joined the moderators to discuss the following questions: (i) Is there a need for the FDA to provide recommendations on the use of modeling and simulation approaches to support the development of generic dermatological drug products? (ii) For a mechanistic PBPK model to be used for virtual bioequivalence (VBE) assessments, how can one adequately account for the inter‐ and intrasubject variability in simulated BE studies? (iii) From a regulatory standpoint, what were the specific considerations relevant to the use of PBPK modeling and simulation that supported the first approval of a generic diclofenac topical gel, a case study presented by the last speaker?
These topics are closely related to the FY21 GDUFA Research Science Priorities, “Complex routes of delivery” which include: “1. Improve Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models of drug absorption via complex routes of delivery (e.g., nasal, inhalation, dermal, ophthalmic) to allow their use in supporting alternative BE approaches, 2. Enhance understanding of excipients on topical drug absorption to evaluate in vitro BE methods for topical drug products applied to skin or other local areas that do not have the same qualitative components (Q1) or quantitative composition (Q2), 3. Implement in vitro methods together with PK and certain other methods as alternatives to the use of comparative clinical endpoint BE studies for nasal and inhaled drug products.”
15
,
16
MEETING SUMMARY
Scientific presentations
Research overview and regulatory experience on mechanistic modeling for generic dermatological drug products
Khondoker Alam, PhD
Dr. Alam opened the session by presenting an overview of the GDUFA‐funded research program, which aims to advance in silico methodologies sought to be employed in the generic drug development as well as regulatory assessment of dermatological drug products.
7
He highlighted that the major focus of the GDUFA‐funded research has been to incorporate a realistic description of skin physiology, formulation attributes, metamorphosis of the formulation, and the interplay between skin physiology and formulation attributes into dermal PBPK models. One of the critical objectives of the GDUFA‐funded research is to realize the capability of dermal PBPK modeling to establish mechanistic in vitro‐in vivo relationships, predict unknown scenarios and perform VBE assessments. Dr. Alam presented the research roadmap of the FDA toward developing mechanistic dermal PBPK models and highlighted the outcomes from these research initiatives. Since 2014, the FDA has awarded eight grants to various academic/research institutes and software developing companies (Table
1
). The workshop attendees were referred to the “
Science and Research Report: Locally acting PBPK modeling
” for a description of ongoing and completed research activities and the outcomes of these research activities in the form of publications, posters, and presentations.
17
In the second part of his talk, Dr. Alam presented the use of dermal PBPK modeling and simulation approaches in the regulatory space. He noted an increase in the use cases of dermal PBPK models over the past several years to support proposed alternative BE approaches involving VBE studies, defining a “safe space” for critical formulation attributes and extrapolating predictions on bioavailability from healthy to diseased populations. Additionally, dermal PBPK models are being used increasingly by assessors in the generic drug program to inform internal regulatory decisions on Abbreviated New Drug Applications (ANDAs), pre‐ANDA meetings, controlled correspondences, citizen petitions, PSG development, etc., as shown by Dr. Alam (Figure
1
).

Toward building a dermal model for
BE
assessment: The role of drug product characterization and performance data
Priyanka Ghosh, PhD
The goal of the second talk, delivered by Dr. Priyanka Ghosh was to discuss how in vitro and/or in vivo data that are routinely generated within the scope of a drug product development program can be leveraged to support both development and verification/validation of dermal PBPK models. Dr. Ghosh explained that the importance of understanding the complexity and the variety of products that fall under the umbrella of dermatological dosage forms that are applied to the skin and key characteristics of such formulations may be considered for building dermal PBPK models. For example, topical dermatological dosage forms include simple solutions which often evaporate rapidly following application on the surface of the skin and could be modeled using an evaporation model embedded into a PBPK model developed for that simple solution. However, products are often more complex with multiple phases (e.g., oil‐in‐water emulsions and water‐in‐oil emulsions). Therefore, more elaborate models capturing relevant formulation components and other product attributes are generally needed to mechanistically describe the metamorphosis of the dosage form and to adequately predict local (and systemic, if relevant) drug bioavailability. Subsequently, the scientific considerations that support the development of PSGs for dermatological products were provided. Dr. Ghosh noted that the physicochemical attributes and structural complexity of topical semisolid dosage forms, and their corresponding failure modes for BE, are systematically considered during PSG development, as the FDA has increasingly focused on developing more efficient product characterization‐based BE approaches supported by GDUFA research as alternatives to comparative clinical end point BE studies for dermatological drug products applied to the skin.
5
,
7
,
18
These approaches generally include a comparative assessment of the formulation, Q3 characterization data, and in vitro and/or in vivo studies comparing a prospective generic product to the corresponding reference listed drug product. In general, the types of studies recommended in a specific PSG depend on the complexity of the drug product.
19
Dr. Ghosh further elaborated that, frequently, a comparative assessment of the formulation, Q3 and IVRT studies may be sufficient for establishing BE of a single‐phase gel; however, additional studies, such as an IVPT study, may be recommended for more complex formulations. The identification of specific Q3 attributes that may be relevant for a given drug product also depends on the complexity of the drug product. For example, characterization of the particle size distribution and polymorphic form of the API in the drug product may be critical when the API is suspended in the dosage form. Alternatively, characterization of globule size distribution may be more relevant for biphasic systems, such as an emulsion. When utilizing the characterization‐based approaches for establishing BE, one key consideration is that the variability in measured Q3 attributes among batches of a prospective generic product should fall within the observed variability for the same Q3 attributes among batches of the reference listed drug product. Last, Dr. Ghosh focused on how drug product characterization and performance testing can be utilized to develop and validate in silico models that can support a demonstration of BE. By utilizing key examples from the research conducted within the scope of the GDUFA regulatory science and research program,
20
,
21
Dr. Ghosh discussed that if the PBPK models were to be used to systematically mitigate risks associated with potential failure modes for BE (e.g., to mitigate the risk of differences in Q3 attributes between a prospective generic and reference listed drug product), then the models need to account for how the Q3 attributes of a dosage form, and its metamorphosis, impacts product performance attributes. In addition, the models need to be validated/verified using relevant in vitro and in vivo data. The talk also discussed the need to assess the sensitivity of the in vitro and/or in vivo techniques that are utilized for generating data; whether the empirical data comes from in vitro studies, or in vivo studies, the quality of the data should be assessed prior to utilizing it to develop or validate dermal PBPK models.
PBPK
Modeling of dermal penetration from topical formulations
Jessica Spires, PhD
Dr. Jessica Spires delivered the next talk and discussed how the composition and attributes of the topical formulation affects the absorption of topically applied compounds into the skin. With an example, Dr. Spires illustrated that PBPK modeling that simulates the mechanisms by which these attributes affect absorption can be used to inform formulation development, reducing the need for animal and human testing. The Transdermal Compartmental Absorption and Transit (TCAT) model in GastroPlus (Simulations Plus Inc., Lancaster, CA) was used to identify critical formulation qualities and attributes of clobetasol‐17 propionate (CP) and to model their effects on absorption into the skin. When applied on the skin, in formulations, such as oil‐in‐water microemulsions, dispersed phase droplets can act as a reservoir for CP to maintain drug saturation in the continuous phase of the drug product. A PBPK model of CP was developed using the TCAT model and validated using data from dermal open flow microperfusion measurements of CP concentration in the dermis following the application of Dermovate topical cream.
22
For model building purposes, information on the composition of the formulation was gathered from published literature, and standard equations were used to model distribution in the skin.
23
,
24
The validated model was then used to investigate the sensitivity of the dispersed phase volume fraction and CP solubility on the local dermis concentration of CP. After exploring the sensitivity of each parameter individually, their combined effect on the area under the concentration versus time curve in the dermis was investigated through coupled parameter sensitivity analysis to simulate a factorial experiment design. Using this approach, a response surface for the two parameters, dispersed phase volume fraction and CP solubility, was derived. Dr. Spires explained that this approach can be used to inform design of generic formulations with the goal of achieving BE.
Modeling and simulation approaches of topically applied drugs to support formulation optimization, clinical development, and regulatory assessment: Case studies discussion
Sebastian Polak, PhD
In his talk, Dr. Sebastian Polak discussed how mechanistic modeling, when informed with formulation parameters and formulation metamorphosis following topical application, can describe the dermal absorption of drugs. Nimesulide (NIM) was used as a model drug to present simulations of in vitro and in vivo experiments and establishment of an in vitro to in vivo extrapolation (IVIVE) toward understanding of formulation behavior and the formulation‐skin physiology interaction, formulation optimization, and clinical development of dermal drug formulation. Dr. Polak explained that a minimal PBPK model for oral absorption, to characterize the systemic disposition of NIM, and the MPML MechDermA model, to describe the in vitro permeation and in vivo topical absorption of NIM, were developed and verified using published data.
25
,
26
,
27
,
28
The Simcyp Simulator version 20 (Certara, NJ) was used for model development purposes. The developed models utilized NIM physicochemical properties, formulation attributes, and physiology information either collected from literature and/or from Simcyp databases (systems data). In the MPML MechDermA model, drug absorption is considered to happen through multiple skin layers via transepidermal and transappendageal (i.e., hair follicles) routes. Dr. Polak elaborated that the in vivo dermal model also considered formulation metamorphosis (i.e., vehicle evaporation and thus subsequent changes in the drug concentration in the formulation layers for three marketed gel formulations: Nimulid gel (reference formulation), Nise gel, and Orthobid gel). The diffusion coefficients and partition coefficients in skin layers were predicted by the reported quantitative structure–activity relationships models published in the literature and built‐in to the MPML MechDermA model. A parameter sensitivity analysis was conducted to understand the impact of vehicle‐related attributes on IVPT data. The stratum corneum lipids‐vehicle partition coefficient in the formulation layer (Kp
sc_lip:vehicle
) was identified to be an appropriate parameter when the model objective is to describe the impact on dermal absorption of marketed preparations, based on differences in their components or composition. Thus, this parameter was optimized for each marketed product based on published IVPT study data.
29
After verification of the IVPT model, IVIVE was performed to assess the predictability of the model for studying the in vivo systemic and skin NIM PKs. VBE trials were performed both at systemic and local exposure levels (dermis concentrations) to compare all three tested drug products with each other. The VBE trials were undertaken as a two‐sequence, two‐treatment, two‐period crossover design. The between‐subject and within‐subject inter occasion (for skin‐specific parameters – surface pH and dermis blood flow, and two general PK parameters – intravenous clearance and volume of distribution) variability were applied in terms of coefficient of variation from the existing default values in the Simcyp Simulator database for Healthy Volunteers. The VBE analysis concluded that these formulations are BE at the level of systemic and local dermis exposure. Dr. Polak highlighted that one of the benefits of the PBPK‐based VBE approach is the ability to identify sensitive formulation parameters that are crucial for establishing BE between a reference and a generic drug product. The work presented showed how the model parameter value for API solubility in the vehicle may be iteratively modified (within the context of testing a virtual formulation variant) to predict partitioning of NIM from the drug product into the stratum corneum and thus test a BE assessment outcome between that formulation variant and a marketed product.
Scientific and regulatory considerations on dermal
PBPK
modeling for virtual bioequivalence assessments and decision making
Eleftheria Tsakalozou, PhD
The last speaker was Dr. Eleftheria Tsakalozou who presented lessons learned on developing, validating, and applying dermal PBPK models for regulatory decision making. These lessons are also summarized in publications on dermal PBPK modeling and simulation approaches.
13
,
30
Dr. Tsakalozou highlighted the FDA's recent approval of generic diclofenac sodium topical gel, 1%, which stands as a successful example of PBPK modeling supporting an alternative BE approach for an ANDA. This was the first time a VBE assessment incorporated into a dermal PBPK modeling and simulation approach supported a “totality of evidence” BE approach that led to approval of a generic drug product. Dr. Tsakalozou noted that the “totality of evidence” BE approach was based on (1) a comparison of the formulation information, as well as Q3 attributes, between the test and the reference listed drug product, (2) an in vivo BE study with PK end points, and (3) a VBE assessment leveraging dermal PBPK modeling and simulation instead of a comparative clinical endpoint BE study in patients. The talk detailed the development, verification, and validation (V&V) of the proposed dermal PBPK model used to demonstrate BE between the reference and the test product. The development of the proposed model involved the integration of data on the API, the drug product and the skin physiology from multiple sources.
13
In order to be used for regulatory decision making, the model was sufficiently verified and validated for its intended purpose. The applicant implemented an innovative two‐level approach for verifying and validating their dermal PBPK model developed for diclofenac sodium topical gel, 1%, which was summarized during this talk. The V&V methodology involved assessment of the performance of dermal PBPK models developed for diclofenac sodium topical dermatological drug products and the assessment of the performance of dermal PBPK models for the reference and test products that were eventually used for the VBE assessment (level‐one V&V). The second‐level V&V aimed at assessing the performance of the modeling platform that was used for model development and included the development and V&V for dermal PBPK models for products with APIs other than diclofenac sodium. Further model refinement that was performed by the FDA aimed at improving model predictions of local bioavailability to meet the expectation that the proposed model establishes a reliable link between systemic (plasma) and local (skin and synovial fluid) diclofenac concentrations/amounts. Dr. Tsakalozou presented a proposed VBE workflow that led up to the comparison of predicted diclofenac sodium exposure profiles locally at the presumed site of action (synovial fluid) and additional skin layers versus the systemic circulation. Considerations and challenges on the implementation of such workflow toward a BE assessment, such as accounting for all sources of variability and adequately capturing the impact of key drug product characteristics on local bioavailability in the case of a fit‐for‐purpose model, were shared. Overall, this talk demonstrated that quantitative tools and methodologies can support alternative BE approaches that involve reduced or no human testing. However, to be used for regulatory decision making and drug product approval, these mathematical models need to be sufficiently verified and validated for their intended purpose.
SUMMARY OF THE PANEL DISCUSSION
In their opening remarks, the moderators outlined the objectives of the session, including the potential drug development applications of dermal PBPK modeling during candidate selection, and when performing VBE assessments, emphasizing that existing product characterization data that is routinely available can be utilized for model building and validation processes. Dr. Raney reiterated that the FDA encourages in silico methodologies being used to support drug product development and regulatory decision making, as illustrated by Dr. Alam previously.
The panelists discussed first the need for the FDA to publish recommendations on the use of modeling and simulation approaches in generic drug development for dermatological drug products. Dr. Sammeta stated that the FDA recommendations in a general guidance would be extremely helpful to the generic drug industry as it would serve as a roadmap for integrating these methodologies into their product development program and subsequent submissions to regulatory agencies. Dr. Zhao pointed out that PBPK modeling and simulation approaches have been used successfully in the new drug space. Dermal PBPK modeling can leverage that accumulated experience along with innovations in the field fostered by the GDUFA I and II regulatory science and research program. The panelists agreed with Dr. Zhao's final comment on this topic that there is maturity and consensus on a workflow that allows for the development and validation/verification of fit‐for‐purpose dermal PBPK models used to inform decision making. Dr. Fang encouraged applicants to reach out to the FDA with their alternative BE approaches compared to those recommended in published PSGs that involve modeling and simulation methodologies if they find the latter to be appropriate for their drug products and responsive to challenges, they might be facing. She noted that the FDA welcomes and encourages early communication with prospective applicants regarding proposed alternative BE approaches; these communications can occur through controlled correspondence and the pre‐ANDA meeting request, for example.
Next, the panel discussed the challenge of implementing intersubject and intrasubject variability when developing a dermal PBPK model. Dr. Spires explained that in the GastroPlus platform, variations in skin physiology between subpopulations and individuals as well as variations in skin physiology between anatomic sites in the human body are considered when performing population simulations. Dr. Polak pointed out that although intersubject and between body sites variability may be relatively well‐managed within the existing modeling platforms, parameterizing between occasion variability, which is relevant within the context of a VBE assessment, is extremely challenging due to the existing knowledge gaps. Dr. Polak explained that methodologies, such as sensitivity analysis, may be used to identify model parameters that impact model predictions. Variability may then be assigned to these impactful parameters to explain observed variability in IVPT and clinical PK data. This workflow is in alignment with the basic principles of mechanistic PBPK modeling. Dr. Arora underlined the need for understanding covariation of key model parameters when developing a model used for prospective simulations. The panel agreed that further research is needed to better characterize different sources of variability related to skin physiology model parameters which will improve model predictability in terms of describing healthy or diseased populations. The potential contribution of clinical studies with replicated design toward quantitatively describing interoccasion variability and understanding the clinical significance of correlating physiology parameters was noted by Drs. Amin Rostami‐Hodjegan and Robert Bies through the chat feature during the panel discussion. The exchange on parameter variability ended with Dr. Fang pointing out that for dermal PBPK models used to inform decisions in the space of generic drug products, incorporating drug product attributes into a drug‐product specific model improves its predictability and applicability.
During the panel discussion, Dr. Tsakalozou discussed the specific considerations that were relevant to the use of PBPK modeling and simulation that supported the approval of a generic diclofenac sodium topical gel, 1%. She pointed out that the modeling and simulation approach submitted in support of this ANDA contributed to a “totality of evidence” approach that led to the ANDA approval. The specific role of the verified/validated dermal PBPK model was to provide a link between local bioavailability (which could not be measured as part of the BE assessment) and systemic bioavailability (which was measured in an in vivo BE study with PK endpoints and submitted to the FDA). The performed VBE assessment showed that the reference and test drug products were bioequivalent at the presumed site of action.
CONCLUSION
The session provided an update on the current status of employing dermal PBPK modeling to support decision making during the development process of dermatological drug products and to support regulatory decisions. Knowledge gaps, and the absence of regulatory guidance for the use of this type of in silico tool, were identified during the panel discussion, highlighting the need for collaboration among all stakeholders.
Take home messages that were derived from the podium presentations and the panel discussion included the following:
The development and application (within the context of use) of dermal PBPK models relies largely on the knowledge and experience gained through modeling and simulation of other drugs and drug products (i.e., oral dosage forms mainly).
Drug product‐specific dermal PBPK models are useful when they incorporate formulation attributes and allows one to study the interactions between formulation characteristics and skin physiology.
Dermal PBPK models are developed and validated using a variety of observed data that include local bioavailability data from in vitro or in vivo studies, and potentially informed by systemic bioavailability data from in vivo PK studies, which are conducted within the scope of a generic drug development program and/or which may be available in the literature.
It is important that dermal PBPK models account for inter‐ and intra‐subject variability for realistic population predictions when they are used for VBE assessments, although characterizing and integrating interoccasion variability into population predictions generated within the context of a VBE assessment is challenging.
Dermal PBPK modeling can be combined with parameter sensitivity analysis to identify informative parameters that may impact local bioavailability and guide formulation design.
Dermal PBPK modeling can be used for formulation development by integrating drug product characteristics into the developed models that are validated against in vitro and/or in vivo data collected for marketed drug products (reference product) and formulation variants.
The regulatory acceptance of dermal PBPK modeling is increasing; these in silico methodologies are being used internally for regulatory assessments by the FDA whereas dermal PBPK modeling has recently supported the first approval by the FDA of a generic diclofenac sodium topical gel.
In summary, the session highlighted that in silico approaches, such as dermal PBPK modeling and simulation, can be (and have been) integrated into the drug development paradigm for topical generic drug products. These in silico approaches are being actively developed to support regulatory decision making in a variety of contexts and remain a major focus of ongoing research to support the development of practical and efficient approaches by which to enhance patient access to high quality, affordable generic topical dermatological drug products.
